title: Rational Functions and the Location of Vertical Asymptotes
author: Muhammad Abdullah Athar
problemStatement: Define a rational function and explain where its graph can have vertical asymptotes. Apply the rule to p(x) = 1/(x^2 - 4) and q(x) = (x - 1)/(x^2 - 1).
finalAnswer: A rational function is $p(x)/q(x)$ with polynomials $p, q$; vertical asymptotes occur at zeros of $q$ that are not canceled by $p$: $\tfrac{1}{x^2-4}$ has asymptotes $x = \pm 2$, while $\tfrac{x-1}{x^2-1}$ has one asymptote at $x = -1$ and a hole at $x = 1$.

steps.title: Define the Class
steps.explanation: Rational functions are ratios of polynomials; every polynomial is rational with denominator 1. Their natural domains exclude precisely the real zeros of q.
steps.why: The definition immediately points at the denominator zeros as the interesting points.

steps.title: Locate Asymptotes via Uncanceled Zeros
steps.mathExpression: q(a) = 0, \ p(a) \ne 0 \implies x = a \text{ is a vertical asymptote}
steps.explanation: Near a zero a of the denominator where the numerator stays nonzero, the quotient grows without bound, so the graph shoots upward or downward beside the line x = a. For 1/(x^2 - 4), both x = 2 and x = -2 are vertical asymptotes.
steps.why: Unbounded quotient behavior is the geometric meaning of a vertical asymptote.

steps.title: Cancel First to Find Hidden Holes
steps.explanation: For q(x) = (x - 1)/(x^2 - 1), the factor (x - 1) cancels, so x = 1 produces only a hole (removable discontinuity) at (1, 1/2), not an asymptote. The surviving factor (x + 1) leaves exactly one vertical asymptote at x = -1.
steps.why: Zeros shared by numerator and denominator vanish from the asymptote list, which is why simplification must come before conclusions.
